subsection: 4. Migration policy in Ireland and the EU

notes.b: Governments balance the economic need for migrants against public opinion and their legal duties to refugees.
points: Aims of policy: to control the numbers admitted, fill labour and skills shortages, meet humanitarian and legal duties to refugees, protect security and support integration.
EU citizens hold free movement rights within the EU; non-EU citizens are third-country nationals whose entry and stay national policy controls.
An economic migrant moves mainly to work or to improve living standards.
A refugee meets the 1951 Refugee Convention definition: a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.
An asylum seeker is a person who has applied for protection and is awaiting a decision, so not every asylum seeker is recognised as a refugee.
The Refugee Convention was signed in Geneva in 1951; its 1967 Protocol removed its geographic and time limits.
UNHCR is the UN refugee agency.
War and conflict force people to flee their country.
Persecution for religion, ethnicity, political opinion or sexuality.
Human rights abuses by the state against its own people.

notes.h: Why EU states attract asylum seekers and other migrants
points: Safety, the rule of law and respect for human rights.
High living standards, jobs and welfare provision.
Existing family and diaspora communities already settled in EU states.
Nearness to conflict zones in the Middle East and Africa, which makes Europe the closest destination for many.

notes.h: Common Travel Area, EU free movement and Irish labour markets
notes.b: Ireland's borders with the UK and the EU are governed by different arrangements, and Ireland is outside Schengen.
points: The Common Travel Area lets Irish and British citizens move, live and work freely between Ireland and the UK. It dates from the 1920s and was kept after the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020.
Ireland is outside Schengen because of the Common Travel Area; Brexit did not end it.
EU, EEA and Swiss citizens may live and work in Ireland without permits.
On 1 May 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to give citizens of the new member states immediate access to their labour markets.
Ireland's labour market was later opened to Bulgaria and Romania, after a delay.
Polish nationals were the largest non-Irish group in Census 2022, at about 94,000.

notes.b: Non-EU workers need a permit, and the system is skills-based.
points: Employment permits are issued by the Department of Enterprise.
The Critical Skills Employment Permit covers occupations in short supply, such as ICT, engineering and medicine, and can lead to family reunification.
The General Employment Permit is the second main type, and a list of ineligible occupations restricts which jobs qualify.
A labour-market test checks that no suitable Irish or EU worker is available.
Purpose: to fill gaps in the labour market without displacing Irish or EU workers.
The Refugee Act 1996 established the original asylum system.
The International Protection Act 2015 introduced a single application procedure, in which all protection claims are considered together.
The International Protection Office decides first-instance claims.
Over 13,000 international protection applications were made in 2022, a record at the time; numbers in 2023 were comparable.
Recent countries of origin include Algeria, Georgia, Nigeria, Somalia and Afghanistan.

notes.b: Direct provision is the accommodation system for international protection applicants while their claims are decided.
points: Applicants receive accommodation and meals in centres, plus a small weekly allowance; the system was introduced in 2000.
Accommodation is now run by IPAS (International Protection Accommodation Services).
Criticisms: long stays, lack of privacy, unsuitability for children, isolation in rural centres and poor mental health.
The McMahon Report (2015) criticised direct provision.
A 2017 Supreme Court ruling found an absolute ban on work for applicants unconstitutional, so applicants gained a right to work after a waiting period from 2018.
The White Paper of February 2021 planned to end direct provision by the end of 2024; the plan was abandoned as numbers rose.
Shortages of accommodation left some applicants without accommodation.
The citizenship referendum of June 2004 (27th Amendment) ended the automatic right to citizenship for children born in Ireland to non-national parents.
About 79% of voters said yes to the 2004 amendment.
Non-nationals may apply for naturalisation after a period of residence, and successful applicants take part in a citizenship ceremony.
The Irish Refugee Protection Programme, established in September 2015, committed to taking up to 4,000 people, including refugees from Syria, through EU relocation and UNHCR resettlement.

The EU Temporary Protection Directive, from 4 March 2022, gave people fleeing Russia's invasion of Ukraine (which began on 24 February 2022) the immediate right to live, work and access services without making an asylum claim.
Temporary protection is not international protection, and Ukrainians are not counted in asylum applications.
Ireland received over 100,000 Ukrainians by 2024.
Housing pressure from Ukrainian arrivals contrasts with the accommodation-based system for international protection applicants.
Policy is open to EU citizens and skilled workers, but restrictive for low-skilled non-EU workers.
The asylum system is slow and accommodation-based, relying on direct provision.
Labour needs pull in one direction and housing pressure in the other.
Anti-immigration protests show public opposition, as described in the notes on Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.

notes.h: Free movement and Schengen in the EU
points: Free movement of workers, from the Treaty of Rome (1957), and EU citizenship, from the Maastricht Treaty (1992), let EU citizens live and work in any member state.
The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 at Schengen, Luxembourg, and came into effect in 1995; it removed internal border checks between members.
A common external border and common visa rules apply across the Schengen area.
The Schengen area had 29 countries from 2025, when Bulgaria and Romania became full members in January 2025; it includes non-EU Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Ireland and Cyprus are EU members outside Schengen.
After 2015 some states temporarily reintroduced internal border checks.
The member state where an asylum seeker first enters the EU is responsible for the claim.
The system is named after the city where the 1990 Dublin Convention was signed; it was replaced by the Dublin II Regulation (2003) and Dublin III (2013).
It is an EU asylum rule, not an Irish law.
It is meant to prevent asylum shopping, where applicants choose the state in which they claim.
It places most pressure on frontier states such as Italy, Greece, Spain and Malta.
The rule broke down in 2015.
Frontex, established in 2004 with its headquarters in Warsaw, is the EU border and coast guard agency.
Frontex runs patrols and returns, and its search-and-rescue role is debated.
The EU Blue Card directive, adopted in 2009, admits highly skilled non-EU workers; seasonal worker rules also apply.
Labour shortages and ageing populations are reasons for admitting workers, as set out in the notes on Changing population characteristics.

notes.h: Recent trends driving policy (2015 to 2016 and after)
notes.b: The main trends behind recent EU policy are the 2015 to 2016 crisis, Mediterranean routes and the Ukrainian movement.
points: The war in Syria from 2011, along with conflict in Afghanistan, Iraq and Eritrea, drove large movements of people.
About 1.3 million asylum applications were made in the EU in 2015, and a similar number in 2016.
Over 1 million people crossed the Mediterranean to Europe in 2015, most reaching the Greek islands from Turkey, with Lesbos the main landing point.
The Eastern Mediterranean route runs from Turkey to Greece, and the Balkan route carries migrants onwards from Greece through the Balkans.
The Central Mediterranean route runs from Libya to Italy; Lampedusa, south of Sicily, is a main landing point.
The Lampedusa shipwreck of October 2013 killed over 360 people and led to Italy's Mare Nostrum search-and-rescue operation (2013 to 2014).
Deaths at sea and smuggling gangs accompanied these routes, and irregular arrivals continued.
The Ukrainian refugee movement from 2022 added to these pressures.
In August 2015 German Chancellor Angela Merkel said 'Wir schaffen das' ('We can do this'); Germany received the largest number of asylum seekers in the EU in 2015 to 2016.
In September 2015 the EU agreed to relocate 160,000 asylum seekers from Italy and Greece.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic refused to take part, and in 2020 the EU Court of Justice ruled that they had broken EU law.
Hungary, under Viktor Orbán, built a fence on its border with Serbia in 2015.

The EU–Turkey statement of March 2016 required irregular migrants reaching the Greek islands to be returned to Turkey; the EU was to provide €6 billion for refugees in Turkey, and arrivals in Greece fell sharply.
Externalisation: deals with Turkey and with Libya and other North African states aimed to control departures before migrants reached EU borders.
Frontex was strengthened and internal border checks were reintroduced.

notes.h: Policy responses since 2022 and the 2024 Pact
points: The Temporary Protection Directive (2001) was activated for the first time on 4 March 2022.
Over 4 million people held temporary protection in the EU in 2024.
The Pact on Migration and Asylum was adopted in May 2024 and applies from mid-2026.
The Pact's main ideas are faster border procedures and mandatory solidarity, under which each state either accepts relocated asylum seekers or pays into a fund.
Ireland chose to opt in to the Pact in 2024.

notes.h: Challenges for EU states from large numbers of asylum seekers
points: Cost of reception and housing.
Slow processing and backlogs.
Integration, including language, jobs and schooling.
An unequal burden on frontier states.
Political division and the rise of anti-immigration parties.
Security screening of new arrivals.
Deaths at sea and smuggling gangs.
Tension between humanitarian duty and border control.
Tension between solidarity between member states and national sovereignty, as the relocation dispute shows.
Europe needs workers but faces public opposition to immigration.

keyTerms.definition: A person with a well-founded fear of persecution in their own country who meets the 1951 Refugee Convention definition.
A person who has applied for protection and is awaiting a decision on the claim.
The arrangement, dating from the 1920s, that lets Irish and British citizens move, live and work freely between Ireland and the UK.
The group of European countries with no internal border checks, a common external border and common visa rules.
The EU rule making the member state of first entry responsible for an asylum claim.
An Irish work permit for occupations in short supply, which can lead to family reunification.
The state accommodation and meals system for international protection applicants, with a small weekly allowance.
Immediate right to live, work and access services for people fleeing war, given without an asylum claim, as used for Ukrainians from 2022.
The EU border and coast guard agency, established in 2004.
The 2024 Pact approach under which each state either accepts relocated asylum seekers or pays into a fund.

factCards.term: Why people seek asylum: three reasons
factCards.definition: War and conflict force people to flee; persecution for religion, ethnicity, political opinion or sexuality; human rights abuses by the state against its own people.

factCards.term: Why EU states attract asylum seekers and migrants: four pull factors
factCards.definition: Safety, the rule of law and respect for human rights; high living standards, jobs and welfare; existing family and diaspora communities; nearness to conflict zones in the Middle East and Africa.

factCards.term: 1951 Refugee Convention: the five grounds of persecution
factCards.definition: Race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Signed in Geneva in 1951; its 1967 Protocol removed the geographic and time limits. UNHCR is the UN refugee agency.

factCards.term: EU free movement in Ireland: the 2004 and later openings
factCards.definition: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens may live and work in Ireland without permits. On 1 May 2004 only Ireland, the UK and Sweden gave the new member states immediate access to their labour markets; Bulgaria and Romania followed after a delay.

factCards.term: Irish employment permits: two types and how the system works
factCards.definition: Issued by the Department of Enterprise: the Critical Skills Employment Permit (e.g. ICT, engineering, medicine) and the General Employment Permit. A list of ineligible occupations and a labour-market test protect Irish and EU workers from displacement.

factCards.term: Ireland's asylum system: the laws and recent numbers
factCards.definition: Refugee Act 1996; International Protection Act 2015, with a single application procedure; the International Protection Office decides first-instance claims. Over 13,000 applications in 2022, a record at the time, and comparable numbers in 2023.

factCards.term: Direct provision: what it is and its criticisms
factCards.definition: Introduced in 2000: accommodation and meals in centres plus a small weekly allowance, now run by IPAS. Criticised, including by the McMahon Report (2015), for long stays, lack of privacy, unsuitability for children, rural isolation and poor mental health.

factCards.term: Direct provision: reforms since 2017
factCards.definition: A 2017 Supreme Court ruling led to a right to work after a waiting period from 2018. The February 2021 White Paper planned to end direct provision by the end of 2024, but the plan was abandoned as numbers rose; some applicants went unaccommodated.

factCards.term: Citizenship referendum, June 2004: what changed
factCards.definition: The 27th Amendment, passed by about 79%, ended the automatic right to citizenship for children born in Ireland to non-national parents. Non-nationals may naturalise after a period of residence and attend a citizenship ceremony.

factCards.term: Ireland's refugee programmes: resettlement and Ukrainians
factCards.definition: Irish Refugee Protection Programme (September 2015): up to 4,000 people, including refugees from Syria, through EU relocation and UNHCR resettlement. Over 100,000 Ukrainians came by 2024 under temporary protection, with an immediate right to live and work.

factCards.term: Irish migration policy: evaluation
factCards.definition: Open to EU citizens and skilled workers but restrictive for low-skilled non-EU workers; the asylum system is slow and relies on direct provision; labour needs clash with housing pressure; anti-immigration protests show public opposition.

factCards.term: EU free movement and Schengen: key dates
factCards.definition: Free movement of workers: Treaty of Rome (1957); EU citizenship: Maastricht (1992). Schengen: signed 1985, in force 1995, 29 countries from 2025. Ireland (because of the Common Travel Area, kept after Brexit) and Cyprus are EU members outside it.

factCards.term: Dublin system: dates and why it broke down
factCards.definition: Dublin Convention 1990, then Dublin II (2003) and Dublin III (2013). Making the state of first entry responsible put most pressure on frontier states such as Italy, Greece, Spain and Malta, and the rule broke down in 2015.

factCards.term: Frontex and the EU Blue Card: border control and legal migration
factCards.definition: Frontex, the EU border and coast guard agency, set up in 2004 with headquarters in Warsaw, runs patrols and returns. The EU Blue Card (2009) admits highly skilled non-EU workers to ease labour shortages in ageing populations.

factCards.term: The 2015–16 migration crisis: causes and routes
factCards.definition: War in Syria from 2011, plus conflict in Afghanistan, Iraq and Eritrea. About 1.3 million EU asylum applications in 2015; over 1 million crossed the Mediterranean, most from Turkey to the Greek islands (Lesbos), others from Libya to Italy (Lampedusa).

factCards.term: Lampedusa shipwreck, October 2013: what happened and the response
factCards.definition: Over 360 people died off Lampedusa, south of Sicily, a main landing point on the Central Mediterranean route. Italy responded with the Mare Nostrum search-and-rescue operation (2013 to 2014).

factCards.term: EU responses in 2015: Germany, relocation and Hungary
factCards.definition: Merkel's Wir schaffen das (August 2015): Germany took the most asylum seekers. The EU agreed to relocate 160,000 from Italy and Greece; Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic refused (ruled illegal in 2020). Hungary built a fence on its border with Serbia.

factCards.term: EU–Turkey statement, March 2016: terms and result
factCards.definition: Irregular migrants reaching the Greek islands were to be returned to Turkey; the EU was to provide €6 billion for refugees in Turkey; arrivals in Greece fell sharply. It is an example of externalisation, as are deals with Libya and other North African states.

factCards.term: EU responses since 2022: temporary protection and the 2024 Pact
factCards.definition: The Temporary Protection Directive (2001) was first activated on 4 March 2022; over 4 million held it in 2024. Pact on Migration and Asylum (May 2024, applies from mid-2026): faster border procedures and mandatory solidarity. Ireland opted in.

factCards.term: Challenges for EU states from large numbers of asylum seekers
factCards.definition: Cost of reception and housing; slow processing and backlogs; integration (language, jobs, schooling); an unequal burden on frontier states; political division and anti-immigration parties; security screening; deaths at sea and smuggling gangs.

factCards.term: EU migration policy: three tensions to evaluate
factCards.definition: Humanitarian duty against border control; solidarity between member states against national sovereignty, as the relocation dispute showed; Europe's need for workers against public opposition to immigration.

questions.prompt: Discuss how recent trends in migration are impacting on migration policy in Europe.
questions.model: Trends: the war in Syria from 2011, together with conflict in Afghanistan, Iraq and Eritrea, drove large movements. About 1.3 million asylum applications were made in the EU in 2015, and a similar number in 2016. Over 1 million people crossed the Mediterranean in 2015, most reaching the Greek islands from Turkey, while the Central Mediterranean route from Libya to Italy brought arrivals to Lampedusa. The Lampedusa shipwreck of October 2013 killed over 360 people. Deaths at sea and the Ukrainian refugee movement from 2022 added to the pressure. Policy responses: Germany's open stance in August 2015 led it to receive the largest number of asylum seekers in the EU in 2015 to 2016. In September 2015 the EU agreed to relocate 160,000 asylum seekers from Italy and Greece, but Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic refused, and in 2020 the EU Court of Justice ruled they had broken EU law. Hungary built a fence on its border with Serbia in 2015. The EU–Turkey statement of March 2016 returned irregular migrants reaching the Greek islands to Turkey in exchange for €6 billion for refugees in Turkey, and arrivals in Greece fell sharply. The Dublin system broke down in 2015, Frontex was strengthened and internal border checks were reintroduced. The Temporary Protection Directive was activated for the first time on 4 March 2022 for Ukrainians. The Pact on Migration and Asylum, adopted in May 2024, brings faster border procedures and mandatory solidarity and applies from mid-2026. Evaluation: policy balances humanitarian duty against border control, and solidarity between states against national sovereignty, while Europe needs workers but faces public opposition.

Irish policy is shaped by the Common Travel Area with the UK, which dates from the 1920s and continues after the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, and which keeps Ireland outside Schengen. EU and EEA citizens may live and work in Ireland without permits, and Ireland opened its labour market to the 2004 accession states on 1 May 2004. Non-EU workers need employment permits issued by the Department of Enterprise: the Critical Skills Employment Permit for occupations in short supply, which can lead to family reunification, and the General Employment Permit, subject to a labour-market test. International protection rests on the Refugee Act 1996 and the International Protection Act 2015, with first-instance decisions made by the International Protection Office. Applications exceeded 13,000 in 2022. Applicants are housed under direct provision, introduced in 2000 and criticised in the McMahon Report of 2015 for long stays, lack of privacy, unsuitability for children and isolation in rural centres. Applicants gained a right to work from 2018 after a 2017 Supreme Court ruling, and the 2021 White Paper's plan to end direct provision by 2024 was abandoned as numbers rose. The 2004 citizenship referendum, which about 79% supported, ended automatic citizenship for children born in Ireland to non-national parents. The Irish Refugee Protection Programme, from 2015, committed to taking up to 4,000 refugees. Temporary protection, activated for Ukrainians from March 2022, gave immediate rights to live and work without an asylum claim, and Ireland received over 100,000 Ukrainians by 2024. Evaluation: policy is open to EU and skilled workers but restrictive for low-skilled non-EU workers; the asylum system is slow and accommodation-based; labour needs and housing pressure pull against each other; and anti-immigration protests show the strain.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly one reason why people seek asylum.
questions.model: People seek asylum because war and conflict make staying in their country dangerous, as with the war in Syria from 2011. Many also flee persecution for their religion, ethnicity, political opinion or sexuality, which leaves them without protection at home. Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a person who fears persecution for these reasons can apply for protection in another country while the claim is decided.
